title: DHA Opens Bidding on CDMRP Research Application Review IDIQ - ExecutiveGov
description:
General Dynamics Information Technology secured the five-year, $171 million award in January 2022 to perform software development and scientific services supporting the peer review of biomedical research grant applications.
That contract served both CDMRP and the Army Medical Research and Development Command, while the new solicitation lists CDMRP under DHA.
How Will DHA Compete Peer Review Task Orders?
DHA will award scientific merit peer review work to multiple vendors through Scientific Administration and Management, or SAM, task orders.
Each peer review contractor will also need to supply and run its own secure online platform to manage the review process from start to finish.
text:
DHA plans multiple-award IDIQ for CDMRP intake, peer review

Offers due Dec. 2 via PIEE; CMMC L1 guidance included

2026 Healthcare Summit to spotlight military health readiness, AI governance

The Defense Health Agency is seeking proposals for a multiple-award indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity contract to support how its Congressionally Directed Medical Research Programs, or CDMRP, receives, screens and peer-reviews biomedical research funding applications.

The Army Medical Research Acquisition Activity at Fort Detrick, Maryland, issued the Biomedical Research Application Evaluation and Support, or BRAES, request for proposals on DHA’s behalf, according to a SAM.gov notice posted Monday. Bidders have until Dec. 2 at 3 p.m. EST to respond, and the competition carries no set-aside.

A day after BRAES proposals close, DHA, Department of Health and Human Services and Veterans Health Administration leaders will share fiscal 2027 contracting priorities at the Potomac Officers Club’s 2026 Healthcare Summit on Dec. 3. Keynote speakers Kimberly Brandt of the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services and Dr. Matthew Memoli of the National Institutes of Health lead a program spanning AI governance, access to care, fraud mitigation and military health readiness. Sign up now!

Who Held the Previous BRAES Contract?

The last BRAES contract went to a single company. General Dynamics Information Technology secured the five-year, $171 million award in January 2022 to perform software development and scientific services supporting the peer review of biomedical research grant applications. That contract served both CDMRP and the Army Medical Research and Development Command, while the new solicitation lists CDMRP under DHA. GDIT said in 2022 that it had supported CDMRP for 27 years.

What Will the eBRAP Awardee Handle?

A single contractor will run the front end of CDMRP’s application process under the electronic Biomedical Research Application Portal, or eBRAP, task order. The awardee will check submissions for compliance, oversee the electronic intake of pre-applications and full proposals from intramural and extramural researchers and configure funding opportunity announcements within the portal. A dedicated quality assurance surveillance plan will govern its performance, and DHA classifies the overall BRAES requirement as performance-based, non-commercial and non-personal services support.

How Will DHA Compete Peer Review Task Orders?

DHA will award scientific merit peer review work to multiple vendors through Scientific Administration and Management, or SAM, task orders. IDIQ holders alone can vie for those orders, which the agency plans to compete under fair-opportunity rules once the base contract is in place. Each peer review contractor will also need to supply and run its own secure online platform to manage the review process from start to finish.

The solicitation package previews that pipeline with sample performance work statements for the eBRAP and SAM orders and for individual research programs such as the Peer Reviewed Medical Research Program. Offerors must also complete a cost-plus-fixed-fee pricing template for a sample SAM task order, along with a labor category and rates workbook.

What Do Companies Need to Submit BRAES Proposals?

Bidders must submit offers through the Solicitation Module of the Procurement Integrated Enterprise Environment, or PIEE, rather than SAM.gov. The module limits submissions to users holding the proposal manager role, and a company’s PIEE account administrator must approve that role after the user registers under the firm’s Commercial and Government Entity, or CAGE, code.

DHA requires each proposal package to include a small business participation commitment document and a subcontracting plan. The agency also attached Level 1 self-assessment instructions under the Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification program. The Department of War kept those self-assessments in place when it suspended CMMC Phase II requirements in July.

DHA listed the contract under North American Industry Classification System code 813920. Offerors must route questions through an offeror question form to points of contact Deanna Moose and Julia Burns.

title: Prepare for TRICARE Open Season 2026: Key Dates and Why You Should Enroll Early
description:
TRICARE Open Season for 2027 coverage runs from November 9 to December 8, 2026.
Its main announcement lists TRICARE Open Season as November 9–December 8, 2026, while a later passage refers to November 10 as the start date.
During Open Season, eligible beneficiaries can enroll in TRICARE Prime or TRICARE Select or change their existing coverage.
Retirees using TRICARE For Life don’t participate in TRICARE Open Season.
TRICARE Reserve Select and TRICARE Retired Reserve also follow separate enrollment rules and are not part of TRICARE Open Season.
text:
TRICARE Open Season for 2027 coverage runs from November 9 to December 8, 2026. Eligible beneficiaries can enroll in or change their TRICARE Prime or TRICARE Select plans during this period, with changes taking effect January 1, 2027.

A September Federal Register notice contains conflicting dates. Its main announcement lists TRICARE Open Season as November 9–December 8, 2026, while a later passage refers to November 10 as the start date.

The notice also lists December 7 as the deadline for FEDVIP enrollment. Current TRICARE guidance and the Office of Personnel Management (OPM), which administers FEDVIP, list December 14 instead.

Who Needs to Review Their TRICARE Coverage?

During Open Season, eligible beneficiaries can enroll in TRICARE Prime or TRICARE Select or change their existing coverage. This includes many retirees and their eligible family members who have or qualify for TRICARE Prime or TRICARE Select. Retirees using TRICARE For Life don’t participate in TRICARE Open Season.

Active-duty service members do not participate in Open Season. The annual enrollment period also excludes beneficiaries enrolled in TRICARE For Life, TRICARE Young Adult, and the Continued Health Care Benefit Program. These programs follow their own enrollment rules.

TRICARE Reserve Select and TRICARE Retired Reserve also follow separate enrollment rules and are not part of TRICARE Open Season. Eligible members can purchase these plans outside the annual Open Season, subject to each plan’s eligibility and enrollment requirements.

What Can You Do During TRICARE Open Season?

During Open Season, eligible beneficiaries can take two main options, depending on their current coverage and health care needs:

Enroll in a plan. If you're eligible for a TRICARE Prime option or TRICARE Select but aren't enrolled, you can enroll in a plan.

Change your coverage. Current enrollees can switch to another eligible plan or change between individual and family enrollment.

Outside Open Season, eligible beneficiaries generally need a TRICARE Qualifying Life Event (QLE) to make enrollment changes. Marriage, the birth or adoption of a child, and retirement from active duty are examples of events that may open a 90-day window. A qualifying event affecting one family member may also allow other eligible family members to change their coverage.

Before submitting an enrollment change, check that your contact information is current in the Defense Enrollment Eligibility Reporting System (DEERS).

"Being able to use TRICARE depends on you keeping your information current in the Defense Enrollment Eligibility Reporting System (DEERS)," TRICARE guidance states. "If you don't show as eligible for TRICARE in DEERS or your information is incorrect, it could prevent you from using your TRICARE benefit. You may also miss important information and enrollment deadlines."

You should also verify your payment information with your TRICARE regional contractor to help prevent coverage interruptions.

What Happens If You Do Nothing?

If you're already enrolled in TRICARE Prime or TRICARE Select and don’t make a change, your current coverage generally continues into 2027 as long as you remain eligible and meet applicable payment requirements.

If you're eligible but aren't enrolled, doing nothing during Open Season won't enroll you. After the enrollment period ends, you generally need a qualifying life event to enroll outside Open Season. Otherwise, you'll only be eligible for care at a military hospital or clinic if space is available.

Check the FEDVIP Deadline Separately

Beneficiaries planning to enroll in or change FEDVIP dental and vision coverage have a different enrollment window from TRICARE Open Season. Current OPM and TRICARE guidance agree on the FEDVIP closing date, but the September Federal Register notice gives an earlier deadline.

FEDVIP eligibility depends on beneficiary status. Retired service members and eligible family members may qualify for FEDVIP dental coverage, including retirees using TRICARE For Life. Vision coverage is also available to eligible beneficiaries who are enrolled in a qualifying TRICARE health plan.

Beneficiaries can use BENEFEDS to check their eligibility, compare available plans and rates, and enroll. Outside Federal Benefits Open Season, enrollment changes generally require a FEDVIP qualifying life event. These events can differ from TRICARE's rules, so beneficiaries should confirm the requirements for their specific coverage.

What Beneficiaries Should Keep in Mind

TRICARE and FEDVIP are separate enrollment processes, so beneficiaries considering changes to both should review each program's eligibility rules and deadlines before making a decision.

Check current TRICARE, OPM, and BENEFEDS guidance as Open Season approaches, particularly if official information is updated before enrollment begins.

"I recommend going ahead and doing it as soon as you make your decision, because you know how life can get in the way of remembering things," military finance expert Kate Horrell advised families navigating Open Season. "Or internet goes out. Or people get sick. We’ve all been there... do not leave this until the last minute."

We asked the Defense Health Agency to clarify the conflicting FEDVIP enrollment deadlines and will update this article if we receive additional information.

title: Pentagon Eyes Outsourcing Tool Sterilization After BAMC Sent 49 Bad Sets to ORs
description:
As reported by the San Antonio Express-News, the Pentagon is seeking private-sector help sterilizing surgical tools after staffing and equipment issues limited the number of surgeries at some military hospitals.
In the summer of 2023, sterile processing problems resulted in the delivery of at least 49 unusable sets to operating rooms over a 41-day span, according to the San Antonio Express-News.
Naval hospitals in Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, and Bremerton, Washington, also experienced sterile processing issues over the prior year, per the Express-News account.
The Defense Health Agency's request warns that a cessation of surgical cases decreases provider readiness, risks citations against graduate medical education programs, and severely impacts healthcare delivery overall.
For now, the Defense Health Agency's outreach remains an information-gathering exercise rather than a decision.
text:
The Defense Health Agency is asking private companies whether they can take over sterilizing surgical tools for Brooke Army Medical Center, Wilford Hall and 19 other military hospitals, after years of contaminated instruments, canceled operations and understaffed sterile processing units disrupted care. The agency says it is not committing to outsource anything yet, but the request comes after a 41-day stretch in 2023 when at least 49 unusable surgical tool sets reached San Antonio operating rooms.

A Business-Case Study, Not a Contract

According to a request for information reviewed by govtribe.com, the Defense Health Agency is conducting a business-case analysis of alternatives to on-site surgical instrument sterilization across eight of its nine networks, including facilities like Walter Reed, Brooke Army Medical Center and Tripler Army Medical Center. As reported by the San Antonio Express-News, the Pentagon is seeking private-sector help sterilizing surgical tools after staffing and equipment issues limited the number of surgeries at some military hospitals. The RFI states plainly that it is a request for information only, not a commitment to issue a contract, and the Defense Health Agency has said it will not award a contract as part of the study itself.

Instead, the agency says it will use the responses to identify qualified, experienced and interested organizations that could provide off-site services in the future, and it has urged healthcare companies and hospitals offering off-site sterile processing to respond. Industry responses to the notice were due March 13, 2026, at 11 a.m. Central time. The RFI estimates a need to sterilize roughly 150,000 trays at each listed military treatment facility, while the Defense Health Agency separately estimates outside providers would handle about 12 types of surgical equipment and roughly 2,000 trays per hospital each month — figures that were not reconciled in the agency's own materials. The requested services would cover everything from transporting instruments between hospitals and off-site facilities to decontamination, assembly, sterilization and quality-control verification, with equipment ranging from minimally invasive surgical cases to power tools, arthroscopy instruments and shoulder-repair sets.

San Antoino Hospital's Repeated Breakdowns

Brooke Army Medical Center's sterile processing team, which cleans and sanitizes thousands of surgical tools every day with a staff of 70, has struggled with recurring failures for years. In the summer of 2023, sterile processing problems resulted in the delivery of at least 49 unusable sets to operating rooms over a 41-day span, according to the San Antonio Express-News. That same stretch saw more than two dozen surgeries canceled outright and at least four procedures delayed by anywhere from 90 minutes to four and a half hours. One patient, per the Express-News, was kept under general anesthesia for an extra three hours because of tool-related delays.

The problems were serious enough that all 19 of BAMC's orthopedic surgeons signed a 10-page memo warning hospital leaders of what they called unacceptable risk, describing contaminated, missing, incorrect and broken instruments reaching operating rooms. Hospital officials maintained they had not identified any surgical-site infections or patient illnesses linked to bioburden or hardware problems in orthopedic cases. BAMC surgeons also reported dozens of additional procedure delays and cancellations between mid-2023 and January 2024 tied to contaminated tools and improperly sealed sets, and the hospital stopped surgeries altogether for 10 days in January 2024, limiting operations through the following month. Hospital leaders cited staffing shortages, including in sterile processing, for the decrease. BAMC did not respond to questions about the current unit's condition, ongoing problems or existing outsourcing, the Express-News reported.

The stakes at BAMC are especially high because it operates the Army's sole Level 1 trauma center and the Defense Department's only burn treatment facility. This is not the hospital's first bout with sterilization trouble — similar problems surfaced in 2016 and again in 2017, when the Army Times reported the hospital shut more than half of its 28 operating rooms and curtailed elective surgeries due to a shortage of properly sterilized instruments, after inspectors found 73 cases of improperly sterilized tools in a single month, including 16 involving organic material like bone, skin fragments or blood left on surgical tools.

Walter Reed and Other Bases Hit Too

San Antonio is not the only post dealing with this. Walter Reed National Military Medical Center in Maryland experienced a steam leak in January 2025 that shut down its sterile processing unit for about two weeks, leaving nearly 270 patients with procedures that were deferred, rescheduled or sent elsewhere. The Defense Health Agency's own account, published by dha.mil, notes that Walter Reed also dealt with a major sprinkler pipe burst that released approximately 60,000 gallons of water into five connected buildings around the same period.

During the disruption, Walter Reed typically completes about 40 surgeries each day, but staffers estimated that number had fallen into the single digits, according to the Spokesman-Review. The hospital had to send instruments to regional hospitals to be sterilized, a process that could take up to two days to get equipment back, and officials expected appointments to be pushed back with non-emergency procedures canceled or delayed for weeks or longer. Naval hospitals in Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, and Bremerton, Washington, also experienced sterile processing issues over the prior year, per the Express-News account.

Why the Pentagon Says It Can't Wait

The RFI itself lays out the stakes bluntly: when sterile processing departments become unusable, operating room and clinic procedures decrease by more than 90%, essentially halting a military hospital's surgical capability. The Defense Health Agency's request warns that a cessation of surgical cases decreases provider readiness, risks citations against graduate medical education programs, and severely impacts healthcare delivery overall. A 2019 federal watchdog review found that officials at five of six selected military hospitals reported having to send patients outside the system for care due to workforce-related challenges, according to the Government Accountability Office, though that finding carries low confidence and predates the current review.

For now, the Defense Health Agency's outreach remains an information-gathering exercise rather than a decision. The agency has said any outside providers brought on in the future would supply transportation, staff, facilities, equipment and quality-control verification.

title: Leidos Awarded $318 Million Defense Health Agency Contract For MHS GENESIS Support
description:
Leidos has been awarded a $317,986,855 firm-fixed-price contract by the Defense Health Agency to provide system reintegration, software licensing, and hosting services for MHS GENESIS, the Department of Defense’s electronic health record system.
Leidos’ responsibilities under the contract include system reintegration, which supports the continued coordination and operation of the different technology components that make up the MHS GENESIS environment.
The Defense Health Agency described MHS GENESIS as a critical defense business system, reflecting the importance of maintaining continuity as the agency moves toward a different contracting and service delivery structure.
The bridge contract is designed to give the Defense Health Agency time to shift services in an orderly manner rather than moving all responsibilities simultaneously.
The Defense Health Agency’s Defense Healthcare Management Systems Contracting Division in Arlington, Virginia, is the contracting activity.
text:
Leidos has been awarded a $317,986,855 firm-fixed-price contract by the Defense Health Agency to provide system reintegration, software licensing, and hosting services for MHS GENESIS, the Department of Defense’s electronic health record system.

The contract supports MHS GENESIS as a critical defense business system and is intended to maintain essential services while the Defense Health Agency transitions portions of the work to other service contractors and establishes more direct relationships with solution providers.

The award was structured as a sole-source bridge contract. During its 12-month transition period, the scope of work is expected to decrease as responsibilities are transferred to other contractors and the government changes how certain technology and support relationships are managed.

text:
Tricare open season is the one time period each fall when beneficiaries can change health plans for the next calendar year without a qualifying life event. Any changes made during the enrollment window take effect Jan. 1, 2027.

But not every Tricare beneficiary can use it — or even needs to.

Who Open Season Covers

Open season applies to people who have, or qualify for, a Tricare Prime option or Tricare Select. Tricare includes the U.S. Family Health Plan and the Tricare Prime Demo among the Prime options.

Who It Leaves Out

Tricare says open season does not apply to five groups:

Active-duty service members

Tricare for Life beneficiaries

Beneficiaries enrolled in Tricare Reserve Select

Beneficiaries enrolled in Tricare Retired Reserve

Beneficiaries enrolled in Tricare Young Adult

What You Can Do During the Window

Tricare lists three options. Beneficiaries can stay in their current plan, enroll in a Prime option or Select if they are eligible but not yet enrolled, or switch plans. Enrolled beneficiaries can also move between individual and family enrollment.

Related: What Is Tricare Open Season? A Guide to Enrollment

What Happens If You Do Nothing

For beneficiaries already enrolled, nothing happens if you don’t make any changes during open season. Tricare says you do not have to re-enroll, and you stay in your current plan as long as you remain eligible.

The outcome is different for an eligible beneficiary who is not enrolled in a plan. According to Tricare, that person is eligible only for care at a military hospital or clinic, and only if space is available.

How to Make a Change

Tricare offers three routes:

Online through milConnect

By phone through your Tricare regional contractor or designated provider

By mail or fax, using an enrollment form sent to the regional contractor or designated provider

Tricare’s Enroll or Purchase a Plan page has the step-by-step instructions and forms.

Missing the Window

Outside open season, enrollment changes generally require a Tricare qualifying life event, which opens a 90-day window to make eligible changes. Marriage, the birth of a child and retirement from active duty count, and a qualifying event for one family member lets all eligible family members change their enrollment.

Related: What Is a Qualifying Life Event for Tricare?

Dental and Vision Run on a Separate Clock

Neither vision coverage for active-duty families nor dental and vision coverage for retirees come through Tricare open season. Both are through the Federal Employees Dental and Vision Insurance Program (FEDVIP), which the Office of Personnel Management manages. Its Federal Benefits Open Season is Nov. 9-Dec. 14, 2026, six days longer than Tricare’s window, with changes also effective Jan. 1, 2027, according to OPM and Tricare. Eligibility depends on beneficiary status, and vision coverage requires enrollment in a Tricare health plan.

Outside that window, changing a FEDVIP plan takes a FEDVIP qualifying life event. Tricare notes these differ in some cases from Tricare’s.

Related: FEDVIP Open Season for Military and Retiree Health Insurance

What Isn't Posted Yet

As of Oct. 19, Tricare had not yet provided cost figures or plan changes for 2027 coverage, so beneficiaries weighing a switch couldn’t yet compare next year's enrollment fees, deductibles or copayments.

Stay on Top of Your Military Benefits

text:
The Pentagon is look­ing to the private sec­tor for help with ster­il­iz­ing its sur­gical tools, a task that has caused prob­lems at mil­it­ary hos­pit­als across the coun­try, includ­ing at Brooke Army Med­ical Cen­ter in San Ant­o­nio.

The Defense Health Agency, which over­sees mil­it­ary health­care, put out a call to industry for altern­at­ives to the on-site sterile pro­cessing depart­ments it runs at BAMC, Wil­ford Hall and 19 other mil­it­ary hos­pit­als across the coun­try.

Sterile pro­cessing depart­ments, such as the 70-per­son team at BAMC, clean and san­it­ize thou­sands of sur­gical tools each day. But staff­ing and equip­ment issues in those depart­ments at sev­eral mil­it­ary hos­pit­als, includ­ing BAMC, have some­times lim­ited the num­ber of sur­ger­ies the facil­it­ies can do.

One recent example occurred in Janu­ary 2025 at Wal­ter Reed National Mil­it­ary Med­ical Cen­ter in Mary­land after a steam leak shut down its sterile pro­cessing unit for about two weeks. Dur­ing that period, nearly 270 patients had pro­ced­ures deferred, res­ched­uled or they were sent else­where. Naval hos­pit­als in Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, and Bremer­ton, Wash., also have had sterile pro­cessing issues dur­ing the last year.

The DHA is explor­ing whether to out­source some work to help ensure unin­ter­rup­ted care for patients at mil­it­ary hos­pit­als.

“When (sterile pro­cessing depart­ments) are unus­able because of onsite equip­ment fail­ure, oper­at­ing room and clinic pro­ced­ures decrease by greater than 90%, essen­tially halt­ing the sur­gical cap­ab­il­ity of the (mil­it­ary hos­pital),” accord­ing to the DHA request.

It warned that “the ces­sa­tion of sur­gical cases res­ults in decreased pro­vider read­i­ness, risk of Gradu­ate Med­ical Edu­ca­tion (GME) cita­tion, and severely impacted health­care deliv­ery.”

Though no con­tract will be awar­ded as part of the study, the DHA said the inform­a­tion will help it identify “qual­i­fied, exper­i­enced and inter­ested” out­fits that could poten­tially do the work at off-site facil­it­ies in the future.

The agency urged “all com­pan­ies offer­ing (sterile pro­cessing depart­ment) off­s­ite ser­vices includ­ing health­care com­pan­ies and hos­pit­als” to respond to the call.

text:
Army leaders are working to give Soldiers and Families more time to prepare for a permanent change of station move and more support once they arrive. At the Association of the United States Army’s Warfighter and Family Forum II on Oct. 13, they described changes to household goods shipments, in-processing, medical care and housing—along with work still to be done.

The forum, “Enhancing the Permanent Change of Station and Onboarding & Integration Experience,” brought together leaders who oversee the transition. Their discussion returned to a central point: A move is not complete when the boxes are delivered. Soldiers and Families also need care, housing and a connection to their new unit and community.

Maj. Gen. Lance Curtis, Commander of the Department of War Personal Property Activity, said the organization reduced a backlog of 18,000 shipments in May 2025 to zero currently. A joint operations center and a single call center help track and resolve moving problems across the services.

Curtis said: “If you leave here today with only two things that you remember, encourage service members, Families and spouses to call 1-833-MIL-MOVE, where they will talk to an active duty service member if they’re having a challenge. We can solve almost any challenge on the spot from start to finish. Or use the website ppa.mil.”

Curtis noted service members with orders can begin booking household goods moves 48 days earlier than previously. They also now have one year, rather than nine months, to file a claim for damaged property, and their spouse or dependent who is listed on their orders can also now file an inconvenience claim. The organization, which is in the process of becoming a full agency, plans to replace its moving system with a new platform that includes mobile tools for vehicle shipments, household goods bookings and claims over the next two years.

After Curtis’ keynote address and audience questions, Sgt. Maj. Ruben Murillo Jr., Senior Enlisted Advisor to the Assistant Secretary of the Army for Manpower and Reserve Affairs, opened a separate panel discussion on the PCS and onboarding experience. Lt. Gen. Charles T. Lombardo, the Army’s Deputy Chief of Staff, G-1, said the Army wants to move beyond sponsorship that amounts to a name and phone number. Using the Integrated Personnel and Pay System – Army as a backbone, the goal is to share information earlier, reduce duplicate paperwork and give leaders more time to welcome incoming Soldiers and Families.

“The biggest thing we can do is get you to your squad leader, your platoon sergeant, your platoon leader,” Lombardo said. Getting pay and housing settled first makes it easier for a Soldier to focus on the unit, he added.

Lt. Gen. James M. Smith, Commanding General of U.S. Army Installation Management Command, said installation personnel offices are working to process orders earlier so Families can plan their moves. His team also reviews Families displaced from housing and monitors how quickly homes are made ready for incoming residents. Smith said the standard between occupants is 10 days, though some homes require more work.

Smith said his team holds housing providers to the turnaround standard. “We hold ourselves accountable,” he added. He also highlighted the Civilian Employment Assignment Tool, which helps spouses working in Army Child and Youth Services seek positions at a new installation before they move.

David H. Dentino, Deputy Assistant Secretary of the Army for Installations, Housing and Partnerships, said tenant satisfaction surveys help determine where housing needs attention. Installations use low scores to develop improvement plans, while the results also inform longer-term investments. Dentino said barracks scored lowest among the housing categories surveyed and outlined efforts to assess barracks conditions, improve heating and cooling systems and identify conditions that could lead to mold.

“Those improvements are directly driven by the results we see in the tenant satisfaction survey,” Dentino said of planned Family housing investments. He urged incoming Families to contact their installation’s Housing Services Office, which can help with off-post rentals, deposits and landlord disputes.

That same advance planning applies to medical care. Lt. Gen. Mary K. Izaguirre, the Army Surgeon General, encouraged Families to review specialty referrals, prescriptions, ongoing appointments and records from civilian providers before leaving. She pointed to Tricare’s moving checklist and said her team is working with the Defense Health Agency to improve the handoff between locations.

Izaguirre said the installation a Soldier is leaving remains responsible for behavioral health care during the move: “They are responsible for your care until you sign in at that new installation.” She encouraged those already receiving behavioral health care to discuss the move with their providers in advance and noted that telehealth may help maintain access during the transition. Izaguirre also highlighted that spouses can now access the Exceptional Family Member Program system and acknowledged that access to older children’s medical records remains a barrier the Army is working to address.

Command Sgt. Maj. Christopher C. Goodart, Division Command Sergeant Major, 101st Airborne Division, Fort Campbell, Kentucky, said reception and integration start when a Soldier is placed on assignment. A six-day reception process brings finance, transportation and other administrative support together before brigades tailor training and introductions to the Soldier’s next unit. The aim is for a squad leader to receive someone who is “ready to go and ready to fight,” Goodart said, while giving the Soldier and Family time to settle in.

The panel also looked beyond the installation gate. Smith said most Soldiers and Families live off post, making local schools, housing providers and community leaders part of the arrival experience.

In his closing remarks, Lombardo emphasized that Soldier and Family feedback will guide the Army’s broader effort to make personnel and transition services easier to access by smartphone. “The most important thing we have is our Soldiers and their Families and that feedback, because that’s going to drive the speed and direction that we go as we continue to modernize these experiences,” he said.

He described a goal of giving Families one place to look for housing, enroll their children in school and manage their transition. Helping Families navigate those changes, he said, can improve their Army experience and help retain the all-volunteer force.

Murillo urged leaders to ask incoming Soldiers what they need and carry that feedback into their work with local partners.

“Know your Soldiers, know what your Soldiers are saying,” Murillo said.
